757.title: The soul of the world
757.hook: an old letter to a man called Diognetus says Christians live in their own countries as sojourners, and are to the world what the soul is to the body
757.carry: every homeland foreign, every foreign land home
757.howItsDone: Some Christians draw on the letter to Diognetus and on 1 Peter's 'strangers and pilgrims' when they talk about belonging to a city while also belonging to God, and some churches pray for their towns and local leaders in their services.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Polycarp, and your line was eighty-six years. Who came to mind when you thought of someone you've stayed faithful to? Day seven hundred fifty-seven.

A man named Diognetus has questions. Who are these Christians? What God do they trust? Why don't they fear death, and why do they love each other the way they do? Somebody sits down and writes him an answer. The letter doesn't sign its name. It doesn't tell us much about Diognetus either. What it does is describe the Christians around it from the outside in, the way you'd describe neighbors to a visitor. They don't live in their own cities, it says. They don't speak a special language. They eat the ordinary food and wear the ordinary clothes of wherever they happen to live. You couldn't pick them out in a crowd. And then the letter says something strange about where they belong.

Here's the strange part, in paraphrase. Christians, the writer says, live in their own countries, but as sojourners. They take part in everything as citizens and put up with everything as foreigners. Every foreign land is a homeland to them, and every homeland is a foreign land. They marry and have children like everyone else. They obey the laws, and in their own lives they go beyond the laws. They're mistreated, and they bless. That idea didn't start with the letter. The first letter of Peter writes to believers, in the King James Bible, "as strangers and pilgrims." Hebrews says the faithful of old "confessed that they were strangers and pilgrims on the earth." The letter to Diognetus turns that old idea into a way of living in a city. Then comes its boldest picture. What the soul is to the body, the writer says, Christians are to the world. The soul is spread through every part of the body, and Christians through every city. The soul lives in the body but isn't of it. The body even resents the soul, and still the soul holds the body together. It's a big claim, and some readers find it too big for any group of people to live up to. Others hear it less as a boast and more as a job description: be in the city, care for the city, and don't let the city be the whole of you. The prophet Jeremiah had told exiles in Babylon, "seek the peace of the city whither I have caused you to be carried away captives." Stranger and citizen at the same time. Not one or the other.
screen: `WHAT THE SOUL IS TO THE BODY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: be a good citizen and a stranger. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind the place you live: your street, your building, your town. Name one thing you could do for it this week, something small and ordinary. A neighbor to check on. Trash to pick up. A local thing to show up for. Then let the other half in: notice one way the place pulls at you that you'd rather not follow. Hold both. If you pray, you can name your town to God, street by street. If you don't, simply wish it well. The bell holds the time.
Diognetus. The man whose questions prompted a letter saying what the soul is to the body, Christians are to the world: spread through it, holding it together, never quite at home.

Your line: every homeland foreign, every foreign land home. Today, do the one small thing you named for your place, and notice where you feel like a sojourner while you do it. Day seven hundred fifty-seven.

758.title: Sunday in AD 150
758.hook: a teacher named Justin explains Christian worship to the emperor: readings, a sermon, prayers, bread and wine, and a collection for widows
758.howItsDone: Christian Sunday services can include readings from scripture, preaching, prayers and an offering; churches differ on how often they share communion.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Diognetus, and your line was every homeland foreign, every foreign land home. Did you do the small thing for your place? Day seven hundred fifty-eight.
screen: `EVERY HOMELAND FOREIGN, EVERY FOREIGN LAND HOME.`

segments.voice: Rumors travel fast about people who meet behind closed doors. So a Christian teacher named Justin does something brave. He writes a defense of his faith and addresses it to the emperor himself. Near the end, he stops arguing and simply describes what Christians do when they gather. No secret rites, nothing hidden. Just the order of a morning. Tradition remembers him as Justin Martyr, and his description gives a window into a Christian Sunday from a time when, as Justin complains, Christians were accused of things they never did. Today we walk into that room.

Here it is, in paraphrase. On the day called Sunday, Justin says, everyone who lives in the cities or out in the country gathers in one place. The memoirs of the apostles, which is what he calls the gospel accounts, or the writings of the prophets are read, as long as time allows. When the reader stops, the one presiding speaks, urging everyone to imitate these good things. Then they all stand up together and pray. Then bread is brought, and wine mixed with water. The one presiding offers prayers and thanksgivings as well as he's able, and the people answer, Amen. Justin even pauses to explain that word for the emperor: in Hebrew, he says, it means so be it. Then the bread and the cup are shared, and the deacons carry some to those who couldn't come. Justin says this food is called eucharistia, thanksgiving, and only the baptized share it. Then the collection. Those who have plenty give what they choose. It's left with the one presiding, and he uses it to help orphans and widows, the sick, those in prison, and strangers passing through. And why Sunday? Justin gives two reasons. It's the first day, when God began making the world out of darkness. And it's the day Jesus Christ rose from the dead. Listen to how familiar it is. Readings. A sermon. Standing to pray. Bread and cup. Amen. An offering for people in need. Churches today arrange these pieces differently, and share the bread and cup more or less often. But the pieces are recognizable. And notice where the collection goes. Not to the building. To widows, prisoners and strangers.
screen: `STAND AND PRAY, THEN BREAD AND CUP.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: picture that early room. Settle, and breathe. See a plain room full of people, some from the city, some who walked in from the fields. Someone reads aloud for as long as there's time. Someone stands to speak. Everyone stands to pray. Bread and a cup go around, and a few pieces are wrapped up for someone sick at home. Notice who's in the room. Notice who isn't, and who's being remembered. If you pray, you can simply join their Amen. If you don't, sit with the picture, and let it be strange and familiar at once. The bell holds the time.
Justin. The teacher whose description of Christian worship shows readings, a sermon, prayer, bread and cup, Amen, and a collection for people in need.

Your line: on the day called sunday. Today, think of one person who couldn't be in the room, the way the deacons did, and send them something: a message, a meal, a visit. Day seven hundred fifty-eight.

what it means: Justin describes a Sunday in plain steps: readings, a sermon, standing prayer, bread and cup, Amen, a collection.
what a scholar hears: Justin's First Apology, chapters 65 to 67, names the day, explains Amen for a Roman reader, and sends the offering to widows and strangers.

759.title: Perpetua and Felicity
759.hook: a young noblewoman and an enslaved woman, both new mothers, face the arena together, and one reaches out a hand to lift the other
759.howItsDone: Christians who keep a calendar of saints remember Perpetua and Felicity together, on one day, and their story is sometimes read or preached then.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Justin's Sunday, and your line was on the day called sunday. Who did you send something to, the way the deacons carried bread to the absent? Day seven hundred fifty-nine.

A father is on his knees in a prison in Carthage, in North Africa. He's begging his daughter. Have pity on my gray hair. Have pity on your mother, your brothers. Have pity on your baby son, who won't live without you. His daughter is Vibia Perpetua, well born, educated, a new mother, nursing her child in a cell. She has been arrested as a Christian. All she has to do is say she isn't one. The strange thing about this story is who tells it. For a long stretch of the account, the words are Perpetua's own: her prison diary, written in the first person, kept by the people who loved her.
screen: `ALL SHE HAS TO DO IS DENY IT.`

segments.voice: Perpetua answers her father with a water jug. She points to one lying nearby and asks him: can that be called by any other name than what it is? No, he says. So, she says, I can't call myself anything other than what I am, a Christian. In prison with her is Felicity, an enslaved woman, heavily pregnant. Felicity is afraid of a quiet kind of thing: that her pregnancy will hold back her execution, and she'll die later, without her friends, among common criminals. The others pray with her, and she goes into labor in the prison. She gives birth to a daughter, and a Christian woman takes the baby to raise as her own. So now there are two new mothers, one free and well born, one enslaved, with nothing in common by the rules of their city, and everything in common by the rules of their faith. On the day in the arena, the account says, the two women are thrown down by a wild cow. Perpetua gets up first. She sees Felicity on the ground, goes to her, gives her her hand, and lifts her up. And the two of them stand together. Before the end, the martyrs give one another the kiss of peace. Churches that remember them still name them together, side by side, the noblewoman and the slave. Some readers notice how much the account pays attention to small things: a jug, a father's gray hair, a woman pinning up her hair in the arena. It reads less like a legend about saints than a diary about people.
screen: `A WATER JUG: I AM WHAT I AM.`
`SHE GAVE HER HAND AND LIFTED HER UP.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: hold someone's hand. If there's someone beside you, a partner, a child, a friend, a parent, take their hand for this minute, without needing to explain. If you're alone, rest one hand in the other, and bring to mind someone whose hand you'd hold if you could, someone who's been knocked down lately. Picture going to them and lifting them up. If you pray, you can hold them in prayer. If you don't, simply hold the picture of the two of you standing together. The bell holds the time.
Christiana sum. The Latin answer Perpetua gave at her hearing, naming herself a Christian. She and Felicity, a noblewoman and an enslaved woman, both new mothers, are remembered side by side.
Your line: sisters. Today, offer a hand, literal or not, to someone the world sorts into a different place from you. Day seven hundred fifty-nine.

760.title: Fully alive
760.hook: Irenaeus: the glory of God is a human being fully alive
760.carry: awake, creative, glad to be in a body
760.howItsDone: Some Christians quote Irenaeus's line in sermons, retreats and books about prayer and creativity, and some pair it with its second half, that the life of a human being is the vision of God.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Christiana sum, and your line was sisters. Whose hand did you offer, literally or not? Day seven hundred sixty.

A few days ago we met Polycarp, the old bishop who wouldn't curse Christ. Here's a thread from that story. A man named Irenaeus writes that he saw Polycarp in his own early youth. He remembers him. Irenaeus grows up to be a bishop himself, and to write a long, careful book against teachings he believes are pulling Christians away from the faith they received. It's a big, argumentative book, full of names and systems. And somewhere in the middle of it sits one short line that people still quote today. The line is today's word.

The line, in its old Latin text, reads gloria Dei vivens homo. Word for word: the glory of God, a living human being. Some modern versions render it the glory of God is a human being fully alive. The words fully alive are a translator's way of bringing out the force of vivens, living. They aren't separate words in the Latin. And the sentence keeps going. Irenaeus adds, in paraphrase: and the life of a human being is the vision of God. So it's a circle. God is glorified when people are truly alive, and people are truly alive when they see God. Why would anyone need to say that? Because some teachers in Irenaeus's world taught that the physical world was a mistake, that the body was a prison, and that real spiritual life meant escaping it. Irenaeus pushes back hard. The one God made the world, he says, and made it good. God works with dust and breath, and the Son of God took on flesh. It's the note the Bible strikes in its first chapter: "God saw every thing that he had made, and, behold, it was very good." For Irenaeus, being human isn't a problem to be solved. It's what God is bringing to life. Christians hear the line in different ways. Some hear it as joy: God delights in people who are awake, creative, glad to be in a body. Others are quick to add the second half, so that fully alive never just means busy or thrilled. For Irenaeus, the deepest life is seeing God. Both halves belong to the one sentence. Neither is the whole without the other.
screen: `AND THE LIFE OF HUMANS: SEEING GOD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: find one thing that makes you fully alive. Settle, and breathe. Notice that you're in a body: feet, hands, the weight of you in the chair. Now let your mind go to something that wakes you up. Not something that keeps you busy. Something that makes you more yourself. Cooking for people. Walking under trees. Singing badly. Fixing a thing. Pick one you could do today, even for ten minutes. If you pray, you can offer it to God as a thank you. If you don't, just hold it, and look forward to it. The bell holds the time.
Fully alive. From Irenaeus: the glory of God is a living human being, and the life of a human being is the vision of God.
Your line: awake, creative, glad to be in a body. Today, do the one thing you picked, on purpose, and notice what it wakes up in you. Day seven hundred sixty.

761.title: The fish sign
761.hook: a fish, two curved lines: in Greek, its letters spell the initials of Jesus Christ, God's Son, Savior
761.howItsDone: Some Christians use the fish symbol on jewelry, cars, signs and church art as a quiet sign of faith, and some teach children the five Greek words behind it.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Irenaeus, and your line was awake, creative, glad to be in a body. What did you do on purpose, and what did it wake up in you? Day seven hundred sixty-one.
screen: `AWAKE, CREATIVE, GLAD TO BE IN A BODY.`

segments.voice: Two curved lines, crossing at one end. That's all it takes. A child can draw it in the sand. It turns up on the backs of cars, on necklaces, on bakery signs and business cards. It tells you, roughly, that somebody here is a Christian. But why a fish? It isn't a cross. It isn't a lamb or a dove. It's lunch. And the answer turns out to be a word puzzle, hidden in plain sight, in Greek.

The Greek word for fish is ichthys. Five letters: iota, chi, theta, upsilon, sigma. Take each letter as the first letter of a word, and you get a creed. Iesous: Jesus. Christos: Christ. Theou: of God. Huios: Son. Soter: Savior. Jesus Christ, God's Son, Savior. Augustine, writing about it in the City of God, spells out the five Greek words and says that when you join their first letters you get ichthys, fish, and that Christ is understood in the word. Then he adds a picture: Christ could live without sin in the deep waters of this mortal life, the way a fish lives in the depths. Earlier still, a North African writer named Tertullian makes the fish a picture of baptism. In his book on baptism he calls Christians little fishes, born in water, following our Ichthys, Jesus Christ. So the fish is a word game, and also a picture of baptism. And it swims through the Gospels too. Jesus calls fishermen: "Follow me, and I will make you fishers of men." He feeds crowds with loaves and fishes. After the resurrection, in John's Gospel, he cooks fish on a beach for his friends. Now, the secret part. Tradition says early Christians scratched the fish on walls and tombs. And there's a story told today: in times of danger, one stranger would draw one curve in the dust, and if the other drew the second curve, they knew they were safe together. It's a good story. The ancient writers quoted here don't tell it. What they do show is a sign whose meaning was explained openly, in books anyone could read. A secret, maybe, mostly in the way a family's private joke is secret. You have to be inside to get it.

Here's the practice: draw the fish. With a finger on the table, a pen on a scrap of paper, or just in the air. One curve. Then the other, crossing at the tail. Then trace it slowly, again and again, and let the five words go by with it if you like: Jesus. Christ. God's. Son. Savior. If you pray, those five words can be your prayer, nothing added. If you don't, just keep tracing, and notice how small a thing can carry a whole meaning. The bell holds the time.
Ichthys. Greek for fish. Its five letters begin five words: Jesus Christ, God's Son, Savior.
Your line: the secret sign. Today, notice one small sign that tells you something to people who know it: a fish, a cross, a word, a habit. Ask what it says. Day seven hundred sixty-one.

762.title: Seed of the church
762.hook: Tertullian tells the rulers of Rome that every time they cut Christians down, more grow back
762.howItsDone: Some churches set aside prayers for Christians persecuted for their faith, and Tertullian's seed line is sometimes quoted when they do.

segments.voice: Yesterday, ichthys, the fish, and your line was the secret sign. What small sign did you notice, and what did it say? Day seven hundred sixty-two.

If the Tiber floods the city, blame the Christians. If the Nile doesn't rise to the fields, blame the Christians. If the earth shakes, if there's famine, if there's plague, the cry goes up at once: Christians to the lion. That's how Tertullian, a fierce, sharp-tongued writer from Carthage in North Africa, describes the mood around him, in a defense of his faith addressed to the rulers of the Roman world. He's writing for people who are being arrested, tortured and killed. And at the very end of that defense, instead of pleading, he says something that sounds almost like a dare.

Here's the dare, in paraphrase. Go on, Tertullian tells the governors. Torture us, condemn us, grind us down. Your cruelty proves we're innocent. And it does you no good. The more often you mow us down, the more of us there are. The blood of Christians is seed. Seed. Not the end of something. The beginning. The version people quote today is smoother: the blood of the martyrs is the seed of the church. Tertullian's own line is shorter, and blunter. Why seed? Some readers hear an echo of Paul, writing to Corinth about the resurrection, in the King James Bible: "that which thou sowest is not quickened, except it die." A seed that's kept safe in a jar stays a seed. One that goes into the dark ground can become a field. Tertullian also says why it works. People watch Christians stand firm, and they start asking questions. What makes them like this? And some who ask, he says, end up joining them. So the very thing meant to end the church starts conversations. Some readers add a careful word here. Tertullian was making a bold claim to the people persecuting him, not stating a law of history, and that the line can sound cold to Christians suffering for their faith today. Others hold onto the line exactly for them: it refuses to let the persecutor decide what these lives meant. Either way, the line keeps one picture in view. A seed in the ground looks like loss. Nobody standing over it can see the field.
screen: `THE MORE YOU MOW US DOWN, THE MORE WE GROW.`
`A BOLD CLAIM, NOT A LAW OF HISTORY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: hold someone suffering for their faith. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind people anywhere in the world who are mocked, jailed or threatened today for what they believe, Christians and people of other faiths too. You don't need names. If you know one story, hold that one. If you pray, you can pray for them in your own way, or simply say their situation to God and leave it there. If you don't pray, hold them in your attention, steadily, for this whole minute, without turning away. The bell holds the time.
Tertullian. The sharp-tongued writer from Carthage who told Rome: the more you mow us down, the more we grow; the blood of Christians is seed.
Your line: seed, not end. Today, when something you care about looks buried or lost, say the line under your breath: seed, not end. Day seven hundred sixty-two.

763.title: Origen reading
763.hook: a scholar and teacher of the young who read scripture on more than one level: body, soul and spirit
763.howItsDone: Some Christians read scripture both for its plain meaning and for what it says to their lives and about God; monastic communities and some prayer groups practice slow, layered reading of a short passage, called lectio divina.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Tertullian's dare, and your line was seed, not end. What looked buried or lost, and did you say the line? Day seven hundred sixty-three.

A teenage boy in Alexandria wants to run out and die beside his father, who has been arrested as a Christian. His mother can't talk him out of it. So, the story goes, she hides all his clothes, and he has to stay home. That's how the church historian Eusebius tells the beginning of Origen's life. The boy writes his father a letter instead, urging him to hold firm. His father is killed. The family is left with nothing. And the boy who couldn't leave the house becomes a teacher, and a reader of the Bible people are still learning from and arguing with. While he's still young, Eusebius says, he's put in charge of teaching people preparing for baptism. Today: how Origen read.

Origen's big idea is that scripture is built like a person. A human being, he says, has a body, a soul and a spirit. So does the Bible. The body is the plain story, the words as they stand, and he says that alone helps simpler readers. The soul is what the text says to how you live: your choices, your habits, your heart. The spirit is what it shows about God and Christ and the life to come. Not every reader is ready for every level, he says, and that's fine. A body is still a body. Then Origen makes a bolder move. Sometimes, he says, the text puts a stumbling block in the plain story on purpose, something that can't work if you take it flatly, to make you stop and look deeper. His example: Genesis counts a first day, a second, a third, with evening and morning, before it mentions the sun and moon. How can there be days with no sun? For Origen, the puzzle is a door, not a mistake. Here's where to be fair. Christians still differ on how to read a passage like that. Some read Genesis closely as history. Some read it as Origen did. Others hold the plain story and the deeper meaning together. And some of Origen's other ideas were later disputed, so churches still differ on how to remember him. But his habit of reading still echoes. Whenever a preacher says this story is about Israel and also about you, they're doing something Origen spent his life on. Take your time with a verse. Ask what it says. Then ask what it says to you. Then ask what it says about God.

Here's the practice: read one verse three ways. Settle, and breathe. Here's a short one from the Psalms, in the King James Bible: "Be still, and know that I am God." First, its body: what is it simply saying? Stop moving, and know. Then its soul: what does it say to the way you're living today? Where are you not still? Then its spirit: what does it say about God, if you're someone who asks that? Take each level slowly, one at a time. If you pray, let the verse be the prayer. If you don't, let it be a sentence you turn over in your hands. The bell holds the time.
Origen reading. A way of reading scripture on three levels, like a person: body, soul and spirit. The plain story, the life, and God.

Your line: read deeper. This week we met a letter, a Sunday, two sisters, a living human being, a fish, a seed, and now a reader. Pick one, and read it again today, slower. Day seven hundred sixty-three.
